facts.fact_text: Following the 2003 Armenian presidential election, the applicant participated in a series of rallies of protest organised in Yerevan by the opposition parties.
On 7 April 2003 at 17h00 a demonstration was held in the centre of Yerevan on the occasion of Mother's Day.
The demonstration of 7 April 2003 took place on the Mashtots Avenue next to the Research Institute of Ancient Manuscripts (Մատենադարան).
The demonstration of 7 April 2003 appears to have been of a political nature, and criticism of the Government and of the conduct of the 2003 Armenian presidential election was voiced at it.
The applicant alleged, and the Government did not dispute, that the demonstration of 7 April 2003 was organised by women.
The applicant alleged, and the Government did not dispute, that the demonstration of 7 April 2003 was attended by about 30,000 people, the majority of whom were female.
Traffic was suspended by the traffic police on the relevant stretch of Mashtots Avenue prior to the commencement of the demonstration of 7 April 2003.
The applicant did not as such participate in the demonstration of 7 April 2003, since most men, including himself, were observing it from a distance, standing on both sides of Mashtots Avenue.
The task of the men observing the demonstration of 7 April 2003 from a distance, including the applicant, was to encourage the women and to prevent possible provocations.

The applicant alleged, and the Government did not dispute, that at the beginning of April 2003 police officers of the Central District Police Station of Yerevan (ՀՀ ոստիկանության Երևան քաղաքի կենտրոնական բաժին) came to the applicant's home while he was absent.
Having found out that police officers had come to his home, the applicant went to the Central District Police Station of Yerevan to inquire about the reasons for their visit.
At the Central District Police Station of Yerevan, the Deputy Head ordered the applicant to stop participating in the demonstrations.

According to the applicant, on his way home on 7 April 2003, about 100-150 metres away from the site of the demonstration, he was approached by two persons in civilian clothes who showed police identity papers.
According to the applicant, the two persons in civilian clothes who approached him on 7 April 2003 took him to the Central District Police Station of Yerevan.
At the Central District Police Station of Yerevan, the arresting police officers drew up a record of the applicant's arrest (արձանագրությաւն բերման ենթարկելու մասին).

The record of the applicant's arrest stated that the applicant had been 'arrested at around 17h30 on the Mashtots Avenue for obstructing traffic and behaving in an anti-social way at a demonstration'.

One of the arresting police officers reported to the Head of the Central District Police Station of Yerevan (ՀՀ ոստիկանության Երևան քաղաքի կենտրոնական բաժնի պետ) that on 7 April 2003 the officers were on duty at the Mashtots Avenue, where a demonstration was being held and a great number of people were gathered.

One of the arresting police officers reported to the Head of the Central District Police Station of Yerevan that while on duty on 7 April 2003 they noticed one person who was obstructing traffic, behaving in an anti-social way and inciting others to follow his example.

One of the arresting police officers reported to the Head of the Central District Police Station of Yerevan that the person observed obstructing traffic and behaving in an anti-social way on 7 April 2003 was brought to the Central District Police Station of Yerevan.
The applicant was subjected to a search at the Central District Police Station of Yerevan during which no illegal items were found.
A record of the search of the applicant was drawn up at the Central District Police Station of Yerevan.
The police officers questioned the applicant at the Central District Police Station of Yerevan.

The police officers drew up a record of an administrative offence (վարչական իրավախախտման արձանագրություն) stating that the applicant had 'participated in a demonstration, during which he violated public order'.
The applicant's actions were qualified under Article 172 of the Code of Administrative Offences (Վարչական իրավախախտումների վերաբերյալ ՀՀ օրենսգիրք) as minor hooliganism.
The record of an administrative offence was signed by the applicant.
The applicant put his signature in the section of the record of an administrative offence certifying that he was made aware of his rights under Article 267 of the Code of Administrative Offences.

The applicant put his signature in the section of the record of an administrative offence marked as 'other information relevant for the determination of the case', where he also added 'I do not wish to have a lawyer'.
The applicant alleged that he had initially refused to sign the record of an administrative offence and requested a lawyer.

The applicant alleged that his initial refusal to sign the record of an administrative offence and his request for a lawyer was the reason why he was kept at the Central District Police Station of Yerevan for the following five and a half hours.

The applicant alleged that during the period he was kept at the Central District Police Station of Yerevan, the police officers were persistently trying to convince him to sign the record of an administrative offence and to refuse a lawyer.
The applicant alleged that the police officers told him it was unnecessary to have a lawyer and spend money for such a minor case.

The applicant alleged that the police officers told him the case had been already pre-decided by their superiors, so a lawyer would only harm rather than help, and that he may end up spending quite some time at the Central District Police Station of Yerevan because of that.

The applicant alleged that the police officers told him that if he signed the record of an administrative offence and refused a lawyer, he would be immediately taken to a court, where at worst a small fine would be imposed and he would be released.
The applicant alleged that he finally succumbed and agreed to sign the record of an administrative offence and to refuse a lawyer.

On 7 April 2003 at 23h00 the applicant was taken to judge M. of the Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan (Երևան քաղաքի Կենտրոն և Նորք-Մարաշ համայնքների առաջին ատյանի դատարան), who examined the case.

The Government contested the applicant's allegation that he was kept at the Central District Police Station of Yerevan for five and a half hours under pressure to sign the record of an administrative offence and refuse a lawyer.

According to the Government, the applicant was kept at the Central District Police Station of Yerevan for two hours and taken to judge M. of the Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan at 19h30.

According to the Government, during the period the applicant was kept at the Central District Police Station of Yerevan, the police officers explained to the applicant his right to have a lawyer and advised him to avail himself of this right, which he did not wish to do.
According to the Government, the record of an administrative offence was signed by the applicant voluntarily and without any objections.

According to the Government, the applicant failed to initiate any actions aimed at the defence of his rights, such as lodging motions or availing himself of other procedural rights guaranteed by Article 267 of the Code of Administrative Offences, despite having been made aware of them.

Judge M. of the Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan, after a brief hearing, sentenced the applicant under Article 172 of the Code of Administrative Offences to three days of administrative detention.

The judge's entire finding in the applicant's case amounted to the following sentence: 'On 7 April 2003 at around 17h00 ... on the Mashtots Avenue [the applicant], together with a group of people, obstructed street traffic, violated public order by making a loud noise, and incited other participants of the demonstration to do the same...'
The applicant's actions were qualified under Article 172 of the Code of Administrative Offences (Վարչական իրավախախտումների վերաբերյալ ՀՀ օրենսգիրք) as minor hooliganism.

Article 9 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 1985 provides that a person shall be liable to an administrative penalty for offences envisaged by the Code, if these offences by their nature do not attract a criminal penalty in accordance with the law.

Article 22 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 1985 provides that an administrative penalty is a form of liability imposed in order to educate the person who has committed an administrative offence to uphold the laws and to respect the rules of socialist way of life, as well as to deter the offender and others from committing new offences.

Article 23 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 1985 provides that administrative penalties that may be imposed include, inter alia, a fine, correctional labour, and administrative detention; the provisions concerning correctional labour and administrative detention are no longer in force as of 16 December 2005.

Article 31 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 1985 (no longer in force as of 16 December 2005) provides that administrative detention is prescribed and imposed only in exceptional cases for certain types of administrative offences for a period not exceeding fifteen days, and is imposed by a court (a judge).

Article 172 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 1985 (no longer in force as of 16 December 2005) defines minor hooliganism as obscene swearing at a person or an offensive annoyance of a person in a public place and other similar actions which disturb public order and peace of citizens, and prescribes a fine, correctional labour, or administrative detention not exceeding 15 days.

Article 223 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 1985 provides that judges of first instance courts examine cases concerning administrative offences envisaged by, inter alia, Article 172 of the Code.
Article 249 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 1985 provides that cases on administrative offences are examined in public.

Article 250 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 1985 provides that the public prosecutor who monitors the enforcement of laws in the context of proceedings on administrative cases is entitled to institute administrative proceedings, familiarise himself with the materials of the case, scrutinise the lawfulness of actions of the authorities in the course of the administrative proceedings, participate in the examination of the case, and lodge motions and make conclusions in respect of questions arising during the examination of the case.

Article 251 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 1985 provides that evidence in an administrative case consists of any facts on the basis of which the authorities establish the existence or absence of an administrative offence and the guilt of a particular person, as well as other circumstances decisive for the proper outcome of the case.

Article 251 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 1985 provides that such facts are established by the record of an administrative offence, the statement of the person against whom administrative proceedings are brought, testimonies of the victim and witnesses, expert opinions, exhibits, the record of seizure of objects and documents, as well as by other documents.
Article 254 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 1985 provides that the record of an administrative offence shall be drawn up by an authorised official.

Article 255 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 1985 provides that the record of an administrative offence shall contain the date and location when and where it was drafted, the post and name of the person drafting it, information concerning the offender, the location, time and essence of the administrative offence, the legal act prescribing a penalty for the offence committed, names and addresses of witnesses and victims if any, the explanation of the offender, and other information necessary for the determination of the case.

Article 255 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 1985 provides that the record of an administrative offence shall be signed by the person drafting it and the offender, and that if the offender refuses to sign, a relevant entry is made in the record.

Article 255 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 1985 provides that when drafting the record, the offender must be made aware of his rights and obligations under Article 267 of the Code and a relevant entry must be made in the record.

Article 256 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 1985 provides that the record of an administrative offence shall be transmitted to the authority (public official) authorised to examine the administrative case.

Article 259 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 1985 provides that in order to prevent administrative offences, if other measures of compulsion have been exhausted, and to ensure the timely and accurate examination of cases and the enforcement of decisions, a person may be subjected to an administrative arrest, search, inspection of belongings and confiscation of belongings and documents, for the purpose of verifying his identity and drawing up a record of an administrative offence, if this record cannot be drawn up on the spot and if such a record is required to be drawn up.

Article 260 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 1985 provides that an administrative arrest must be recorded, and the record must indicate the date and place, the post and the name of the person drawing up the record, information about the arrestee, and the time, place and grounds of the arrest.

Article 261 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 1985 provides that only authorities (officials) authorised by the laws of the USSR and Armenia can impose an administrative arrest on a person who has committed an administrative offence, including the internal affairs authorities in cases of minor hooliganism.

Article 267 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 1985 provides that the person against whom administrative proceedings are brought has the right to familiarise himself with the materials of the case, to make statements, to submit evidence, to lodge motions, and to have legal assistance during the examination of the case.

Article 271 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 1985 provides that any person who may be aware of any circumstance connected to the case which needs to be clarified may be called as a witness in an administrative case.

Article 277 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 1985 provides that cases concerning administrative offences envisaged under, inter alia, Article 172 of the Code shall be examined within one day.

Article 278 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 1985 provides that at the hearing the examining authority announces the case to be examined and the person against whom administrative proceedings are brought, explains to the persons participating in the case their rights and obligations, reads out the record of an administrative offence, hears the persons participating in the case, examines the evidence and rules on motions, and if a public prosecutor participates, hears his opinion.

Article 279 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 1985 provides that in examining the administrative case, the authority must clarify whether an administrative offence has been committed, whether the person in question is guilty of committing it, whether an administrative penalty should be imposed, whether there are mitigating and aggravating circumstances, and whether pecuniary damage has been caused.

Article 286 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 1985 provides that the court's (the judge's) decision to impose an administrative penalty is final and not subject to appeal in administrative proceedings, except for the cases prescribed by law.
Article 289 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 1985 provides that the prosecutor can lodge a protest against the decision taken on an administrative case.

Article 294 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 1985 provides that the judge's decision to impose an administrative penalty for an offence envisaged under, inter alia, Article 172 of the Code can be quashed or modified by the judge himself upon a protest of the prosecutor and, whether or not such a protest is lodged, by the chairman of the superior court.

Article 5 of the Law on the Status of a Judge (Դատավորի կարգավիճակի մասին ՀՀ օրենք) provides that in administering justice, a judge is independent and obeys only the law, and is not accountable to any public authority or a public official.

Article 6 of the Law on the Status of a Judge provides that any interference by public authorities, bodies of local self-government and their officials, political parties, non-governmental associations and media with a judge's performance of his functions of administering justice is impermissible and leads to accountability prescribed by law.

Article 6 of the Law on the Status of a Judge provides that a judge is not obliged to give explanations concerning a case or the substance of materials under his consideration or to grant access to them other than in cases and according to a procedure prescribed by law.

Traffic was suspended by the traffic police on the relevant stretch of Mashtots Avenue prior to the commencement of the demonstration of 7 April 2003.

The record of the applicant's arrest stated that the applicant had been 'arrested at around 17h30 on the Mashtots Avenue for obstructing traffic and behaving in an anti-social way at a demonstration'.

One of the arresting police officers reported to the Head of the Central District Police Station of Yerevan that while on duty on 7 April 2003 they noticed one person who was obstructing traffic, behaving in an anti-social way and inciting others to follow his example.

One of the arresting police officers reported to the Head of the Central District Police Station of Yerevan that the person observed obstructing traffic and behaving in an anti-social way on 7 April 2003 was brought to the Central District Police Station of Yerevan.

Judge M. of the Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan, after a brief hearing, sentenced the applicant under Article 172 of the Code of Administrative Offences to three days of administrative detention.

The judge's entire finding in the applicant's case amounted to the following sentence: 'On 7 April 2003 at around 17h00 ... on the Mashtots Avenue [the applicant], together with a group of people, obstructed street traffic, violated public order by making a loud noise, and incited other participants of the demonstration to do the same...'

According to the record of the court hearing — drawn up in calligraphic handwriting — the hearing in the applicant's case was held in public with the participation of the judge, a clerk and the applicant.
According to the record of the court hearing, the judge explained the applicant's rights to him and informed him of the possibility to challenge the judge and the clerk.
According to the record of the court hearing, the applicant did not wish to lodge any challenges.
According to the record of the court hearing, the applicant stated that he was aware of his rights and did not wish to have a lawyer.
According to the record of the court hearing, the judge read out the motion submitted by the police, seeking to impose administrative liability on the applicant.
According to the record of the court hearing, the applicant stated that he, together with a group of unknown people, had blocked the traffic on the Mashtots Avenue.
According to the record of the court hearing, the applicant said that he blocked traffic because it was a demonstration and everybody else was doing the same.
According to the record of the court hearing, the applicant said he made noise since everybody else was making noise, but he did not push anybody.
According to the record of the court hearing, no questions were put to the applicant.
According to the record of the court hearing, the judge read out and examined the materials prepared by the police.

According to the record of the court hearing, having familiarised himself with the materials prepared by the police, the applicant accepted that he had signed the record of an administrative offence but objected to being subjected to administrative liability since the incriminated acts had been committed also by others.
According to the record of the court hearing, the judge departed to the deliberation room, after which he returned and announced the decision.

The applicant alleged, and the Government did not explicitly dispute, that the record of the court hearing was a fake and was drafted at some point after the hearing in order to create an appearance of lawfulness.
The applicant alleged that in reality there was no clerk at the hearing and the hearing was not being recorded.
The applicant alleged that the hearing lasted only about five minutes and was conducted in judge M.'s office.
The applicant alleged that, contrary to what the record of the court hearing stated, only judge M., the applicant and the accompanying police officer were present at the hearing.
The applicant alleged that the accompanying police officer did not as such participate in the hearing and his functions were limited only to bringing the applicant before judge M.
The applicant alleged that judge M. listed the materials prepared by the police and asked the applicant 'what do you want?', to which the applicant replied 'Justice and lawfulness'.

The applicant alleged that judge M. continued reading through the materials and said 'since you have three children and have not been guilt-stained in the past, I will impose a mild sentence of three days of detention'.
The applicant alleged that in reply he tried to present the circumstances of the case, petitioned judge M. to summon some witnesses and requested a lawyer.

The applicant alleged that judge M. listened silently to the applicant, signed some papers and let the applicant go, after which the applicant was taken to a detention centre where he served his sentence.

Article 26 of the Constitution of Armenia of 1995 (prior to the amendments introduced in 2005) provides that citizens have the right to hold peaceful assemblies, rallies, processions and demonstrations without carrying arms.
Article 24 of the Constitution of Armenia of 1995 (prior to the amendments introduced in 2005) provides that everyone has the right to express his opinion.
Article 24 of the Constitution of Armenia of 1995 (prior to the amendments introduced in 2005) provides that it is prohibited to force anyone to give up or change his opinion.

Article 24 of the Constitution of Armenia of 1995 (prior to the amendments introduced in 2005) provides that everyone has the right to freedom of expression, including the freedom to seek, receive and impart information and ideas through any information medium regardless of frontiers.
